articles.title: Israel election double standard: Arab leader forced out, far right cleared
articles.summary: Palestinian Israeli leader forced to withdraw candidature while far-right Israeli leaders allowed to run in polls.
articles.body:
A prominent Palestinian Israeli politician has been forced to withdraw from the upcoming elections over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their incendiary rhetoric and calls for violence against Palestinians.

The Israeli political institutions, including the electoral body, have been accused of double standards for targeting Palestinian politicians and parties in Israel.

Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of the Balad party, withdrew his candidacy after the Supreme Court warned he could be disqualified from the race. He has described the decision to disqualify him from the upcoming elections as “a historical catastrophe for democracy”.

That court advisory came after Israel’s central elections committee barred him from running over comments he made about the war on Gaza.

The election, set for October 27, has renewed scrutiny of the challenges faced by Palestinian citizens of Israel seeking political representation.

Experts and critics, including Palestinian rights groups, have accused electoral system staff of applying a double standard in which Arab candidates have faced attempts to remove them from the ballot, while far-right Israeli politicians accused of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians have been allowed to run.

“It’s always been the case whether the Israeli political system, the political elite, has always designed the political system in a way to ensure that it’s a Zionist state, not just or even a Jewish state,” Zaidon Alkinani, founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, told Al Jazeera.

So, what happened, and what does the controversy say about Palestinian participation in Israeli elections?

Abu Shehadeh is a historian from Jaffa and the leader of Balad, a Palestinian nationalist party that advocates equal rights for all citizens of Israel. He served in the Knesset from 2019 until 2022.

His candidacy was challenged by far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir over an article published on October 8, 2023, the day after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which he described as “an important historical event”.

Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara backed his disqualification , arguing the wording could amount to support for armed struggle.

Abu Shehadeh, speaking at the Supreme Court on Thursday, said he did not support “armed struggle”, but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. The Balad leader said his intention was to urge moving the conflict towards a political process.

What was the Israeli Supreme Court’s decision?

Last month, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Abu Shehadeh, Hadash politician Ofer Cassif and the two main Arab-majority electoral lists – the Joint List, which includes Balad, Hadash and Ta’al, and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.

The Supreme Court overturned the bans on the two lists and Cassif.

Cassif is a politician from the left-wing, Arab-majority Hadash-Ta’al party. In the late 1980s, the pro-Palestinian Israeli spent time in jail for refusing to serve as a soldier in the occupied territories.

He claimed in 2021 that police beat him while he participated in a protest against an illegal Jewish settlement in occupied East Jerusalem.

Abu Shehadeh accused the Supreme Court of bowing to pressure from Ben-Gvir and questioned how a politician he accused of promoting violence and displacement against Palestinians could seek his exclusion from the election.

“Someone [Ben-Gvir] who was calling for starving people to death in Gaza, for preventing medicine, water and food, and supports the occupation and ethnic cleansing in the [occupied] West Bank … was able to disqualify me, a human rights activist for three decades,” Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera.

Adalah, the legal rights group representing him, called his withdrawal “a severe blow” to Palestinian citizens’ right to political representation.

“This entire process was a deliberate attempt to delegitimise Palestinian citizens and their parliamentary representatives and to turn racism against Palestinians into election propaganda,” it said in a media statement.

Have Israeli leaders used incendiary language?

Before the Supreme Court hearings, petitions were also submitted seeking to disqualify the parties of Ben-Gvir and that of another far-right cabinet member, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

The Central Elections Committee rejected those petitions, leaving both parties on the ballot.

Section 7A of Israel’s Basic Law on the Knesset provides the legal grounds for barring candidates or electoral lists, including rejecting Israel’s character as a “Jewish and democratic state”, promoting racism, or backing an armed campaign against Israel by a hostile state or a designated “terrorist” group.

Attorney General Baharav-Miara found that the attempts to exclude the far-right parties lacked sufficient legal basis.

Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have repeatedly faced international backlash over their incendiary rhetoric towards Palestinians. In 2025, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway imposed sanctions on both ministers, accusing them of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

More recently, Ben-Gvir proposed a seven-year plan for Palestinians to leave Gaza through what he called “voluntary emigration”.

“Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now,” he said in September. “Instead of [them] digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases.”

Smotrich has also advocated the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and annexation of the occupied West Bank. Both he and Ben-Gvir have called for the permanent takeover of Gaza and re-establishment of Jewish settlements there, proposals Netanyahu has rejected.

Why are there accusations of a double standard?

The different treatment of Abu Shehadeh and Israel’s far-right politicians has led Palestinian politicians and experts to accuse the electoral system of applying a double standard.

Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najjar told Al Jazeera that Abu Shehadeh’s case exposed what he described as the “two-tier nature of Israeli democracy”.

“This is not the equal application of the law,” he said. “It establishes one threshold for Jewish Israeli politicians and another for Palestinian citizens of Israel.”

Najjar pointed to the contrast between the court’s treatment of Abu Shehadeh’s October 2023 article and the continued eligibility of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, despite inflammatory statements attributed to the two far-right politicians.

“Jewish extremism can be accommodated within Israel’s political system,” Najjar argued, “while Palestinian political speech is treated as an existential threat”.

“A democracy that selectively excludes Palestinian representatives cannot credibly call itself democratic.”

Alkinani, founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, argued the controversy reflected a wider problem facing Palestinian political participation rather than an isolated dispute over one candidate.

He told Al Jazeera that Israel’s political system had historically been structured to preserve its Zionist character, creating particular “intimidation” and “pressures” for Palestinian citizens seeking political representation.

Alkinani said those pressures had intensified since October 7, 2023, which he argued had given a “powerful symbolic push and confidence” to right-wing nationalist parties.

What are the difficulties facing Palestinians in Israeli elections?

Attempts to exclude Palestinian-led parties are not new.

Adalah has documented challenges to Arab candidates or lists in elections in 2003, 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2022. The Supreme Court has repeatedly overturned decisions by the Central Elections Committee, whose voting members are representatives of parties in the outgoing Knesset.

Palestinian citizens of Israel account for roughly 20 percent of the population, yet their turnout at the polls has traditionally been lower than that of Jewish Israelis.

Parties must also secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter parliament, encouraging smaller Arab parties to form joint lists to avoid losing representation altogether.

Arab Perspectives Institute’s Alkinani says the issue extended beyond Israel’s far right. Some parties considered centrist on domestic Israeli issues, he said, still supported “hawkish security actions towards the Palestinians”.

articles.title: Teaching is just the start: The crushing burden on India's college teachers
articles.summary: In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway.
articles.body: In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway. At the front, a professor moves through a technical lesson while also keeping track of attendance sheets and administrative requirements.In the middle rows, a student sits quietly, mentally calculating train schedules between Bengaluru and Pune. He is trying to work out how to explain to a corporate employer that a career-launching Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) could be at risk because of a mandatory offline attendance requirement for a single elective subject.The scene captures a growing tension inside India’s higher education system.For final-year students, college is no longer only about completing a degree. With competition for jobs intensifying, students are increasingly focused on internships, practical skills, early employment and mental health support. But the institutional framework around them remains tied to attendance thresholds, credit requirements, standardised evaluation and administrative compliance.Caught at the centre of these competing pressures is the college teacher.According to data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), while recommended Student-Teacher Ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 or more students per section.The pressure is compounded by faculty shortages. Central universities report faculty vacancy rates between 29% and 34%, while senior professor vacancies frequently exceed 50%. Across technical institutions such as the IITs, NITs and IIITs, unfilled positions range from 30% to over 50%.This leaves teachers performing several roles at once: academic instructors, institutional policy enforcers, career advisers and, often, informal listeners when students are struggling.At the same time, they have to manage UGC Academic Performance Indicators, NAAC and NIRF documentation and heavy teaching loads.Modern classroom: More than academicsFor today's students, particularly those in their final year, the classroom is closely linked to the question of what happens after graduation.“A student may come because he is confused about an internship, worried about placements or simply doesn't know how to deal with something happening at home. We try to listen, but there is a limit to what a subject teacher can realistically handle,” Prakash, a college faculty member at an engineering college says.From the student's perspective, the final year can feel like a race against time, with academic requirements running alongside internships, placements and preparations for entering the workforce.Pranav Vats, a final-year Computer Science and Engineering student in Bengaluru, describes what students prioritise:“Whenever a guy comes to a college, he eventually wants to get placed. He doesn't want to get a 9 plus CGP every semester. He just wants to get placed in a good company and do well in his career financially and also growth-wise... I have been doing internships from the first year itself. And whatever interviews I have been going through, nobody asked me about what my CGPA is. Everybody just asked, okay, how much do you know, how much practical skills you have, and how well you understand the market and how well do you understand your business in which you are going to work now.”That shift creates a difficult balance for teachers. Students may see practical experience as more directly connected to employment, while faculty members remain responsible for ensuring that students complete prescribed courses, credits and attendance requirements.When attendance collide with careerThe tension becomes particularly visible during placement and internship season.Pranav describes a situation in which he had secured an internship opportunity in Pune after clearing an interview:“Two, three months back, I got an interview. I've cleared it. I went to Pune. And at that time, I got permission from college. They gave me this letter of acknowledgement that you can go and pursue your six months internship, and all. But all of a sudden, after two months, they are saying that no, you have to fulfil your academic requirements and all... This company is very good. I'm doing very well there. And they are giving me the PPO for it. I could have got placed. But right now, this company is not giving away. College is saying that you have to attend weekly once class. As a student, it is not possible for me to come from Pune to Bangalore every week to attend some stupid class that is not even relevant to my coursework, which is not even relevant to my computer science degree... It is just an open elective subject.”He says discussions with his mentor, department head and other authorities did not resolve the problem.“What they said to me is, ‘No, do you want your graduate certificate or you want your internship certificate? So fulfill your graduation thing first, then you go and do whatever you want to do.’ They just want, basically, to fulfill what the college needs. And apart from that, you can do whatever you want to do. We don't care.”Pranav says similar situations have affected other students, including those with jobs or internships in Bengaluru itself.He says, “There is this one guy who got placed in Nokia in Bangalore itself. And he said, ‘Sir, I can't attend this class this week because I've got placed here at Nokia.’ They said, ‘You have to do it. I don't care. You have to fulfill this academic thing’.”For teachers, however, understanding the student's situation does not necessarily mean being able to change the rule.“The final year is particularly difficult because everything seems to happen at once. Students are completing projects, dealing with attendance and examinations, and at the same time worrying about placements and what they are going to do after graduation. You can see that pressure building up, especially when a student's plans don't work out,” the faculty said.The faculty member explains the dilemma:“There are situations where a student gets an internship or an opportunity outside the college and genuinely needs flexibility. As a teacher, you may understand why that opportunity matters to him. But you are also responsible for implementing the academic requirements. That can put the teacher in an uncomfortable position because you may sympathise with the student without having the authority to change the rule.”Teacher becomes institutional bufferThe teacher is therefore often caught between three sets of expectations.The administration expects attendance, syllabus completion and documentation for institutional requirements. Students expect empathy, career guidance and flexibility. Parents expect academic performance, safety and career outcomes.The teacher may have to explain an institutional decision to a student without having any authority over that decision.“Sometimes the student is upset with the institution, the parents are worried about the student's performance and the department is concerned about academic requirements,” the teacher explains. “The teacher ends up sitting in the middle. We are expected to explain one side to the other, even though we may not have control over the decision ourselves.”For students, this can reinforce the perception that teachers are primarily there to enforce attendance and award marks.Pranav puts it bluntly, “They don't care, they just want these things to attend classes, they want attendance, they want marks, that's it... If you go to an off-campus thing, where majorly everybody is applying right now, nobody asks you about your CGPA. They just want you to have your practical skills. But this CGPA thing or whatever coursework they are teaching us in college, it is not even relevant to what we will work in our offices.”When personal problems enter classroomThe pressure is not limited to academics and placements.Teachers are also increasingly expected to recognise when students are struggling emotionally, even though they may not be trained to provide professional mental health support.“You spend enough time with a class to notice changes,” the faculty member observes. “If a student who is normally interactive suddenly stops speaking, misses classes or stops submitting work, you notice it. The difficult part is deciding whether to ask, ‘Is everything okay?’ because you don't know whether the student wants you to enter that part of his life,” Prakash say.The teacher describes the boundary involved, “There is a very fine line between being concerned about a student and becoming intrusive. If I ask too many questions, it may seem intrusive. If I don't ask anything, I may miss something important. Teachers are constantly trying to judge where that line is.”At the same time, faculty members recognise their own limitations.“I want my students to know that they can approach me, but I also have to be honest about my limitations. I can listen, I can help them think through a problem and I can direct them towards the right person. But I am not trained to provide therapy, and pretending otherwise can be harmful,” Prakash says.Counselling gap, a stigma problemMany institutions have counselling cells or mentor-mentee systems, but having a service does not necessarily mean students will use it.Pranav says his mentor-mentee system is largely focused on academic issues:“For every 20 or 30 sets of people there is assigned one mentor. So whatever the issues you have regarding the college, you can talk with them and they can get a resolution about it... [But] there is nothing like that through which we can discuss our career... They are strictly for the subject.”He says students also face peer pressure around seeking counselling.“We have one basically like they have hired a person... if you have any emotional issues or something like that, then you can go schedule a session,” Pranav says. “[But] if you suppose you go to a counsellor there is this peer pressure. If you go to a counselor, or maybe you're discussing things with the teacher, you would seem like a weak person.”“This thing is very very disturbing to the students and nobody talks about it because everybody feels that okay, if I talk about it I can feel weak about it and people will think that okay he's not mature enough to deal with his own problem on his own... I talk to some of my friends about it who are eventually on the same path... but majorly I work with my pressure on my own,” Pranav adds.When behaviour changes significantly, teachers also have to balance intervention with confidentiality.“If I feel that a student's behaviour has changed significantly, I cannot just say, ‘That's his personal matter.’ There are situations where you have to involve the appropriate support system. But you also have to be careful about confidentiality and about not turning a student's difficulty into a public issue,” Prakash says.Emotional burden on teachersWhile student stress receives increasing attention, the pressure on faculty can remain largely invisible.A teacher managing a class of 80 to 120 students may also have to deal with staff shortages, administrative work, evaluations, meetings and institutional documentation. A difficult conversation with a student does not necessarily end when the class does.The faculty member says teachers need institutional support if they are expected to take on these additional responsibilities.Prakash says, “I don't think teachers are unwilling to take on a larger role. Most teachers care about what happens to their students. But if the expectation is that we should identify emotional distress, provide career guidance, handle academic problems and support students through personal crises, then the institution also has to give teachers training and a proper support structure.”Beyond the classroomThe experiences of both students and teachers point to a larger structural problem.When colleges rely on individual teachers to enforce academic rules, handle administrative requirements, guide students through careers and respond to emotional distress, the teacher becomes the point where multiple pressures meet.The solution therefore cannot rest entirely on individual faculty members.As colleges respond to changing job markets and rising student pressures, the system would require clearer boundaries for faculty responsibilities, greater flexibility for final-year students navigating legitimate career opportunities, and stronger professional support systems.For the teacher standing at the front of the classroom, the challenge is no longer simply teaching the subject. It is managing everything that happens around it, often without the authority, time or institutional support required to do so.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
articles.summary: Polls show tight race between incumbent Lula and right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro amid concerns over crime and economy.
articles.body:
For the second election in a row, Brazilian voters face a choice between left-wing candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family .

The country’s fractious election is set to take place during a wave of successful far-right candidates across Latin America and a sensitive time in Brazil’s modern political history.

Former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his loss to Lula in 2022. The conviction of Jair Bolsonaro and several military officers raised questions about the resilience of Brazilian democracy, revived several decades ago following a period of rule by a United States-backed military dictatorship.

An explosive corruption scandal has implicated prominent figures and institutions across the political spectrum, and observers have expressed concern about possible US intervention .

Polls suggest Lula, the current president seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off.

Who are the candidates, what issues have been front and centre, and what could the election mean for Brazil? Here’s what you need to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential elections.

The first round of voting in the Brazilian presidential election will take place on October 4 from 8am to 5pm Brasilia time (11:00 to 20:00 GMT).

If no candidate wins the first round outright, the top two candidates will proceed to a run-off vote on October 25.

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva , better known simply as Lula, is the country’s current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT.

The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and his current term, which began in 2023.

His time in office has been defined by an effort to pair political democracy, restored after a US-backed military dictatorship that ruled the country for several decades until the 1980s, with material improvement for the country’s poor through a series of social programmes meant to address inequality.

Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage .

“He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call.

Flavio Bolsonaro has emerged as the heir to his father’s status as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger in the 2026 election. Bolsonaro is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.

The 45-year-old is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Flavio has pledged a hard stance on crime and insecurity and close collaboration with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”.

He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.

Flavio Bolsonaro has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison.

“I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September.

“The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” said Pagliarini.

“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added.

As with many recent elections across the region, crime, insecurity and cost of living issues have dominated the Brazilian election. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign.

A Quaest survey from September 7 found that 31 percent of respondents cited violence as their biggest concern, followed by 20 percent who said corruption, 19 percent who said the economy, and 12 percent who said health.

While Brazil has seen decent economic growth and low unemployment and inflation during Lula’s third term, those mild gains have been paired with explosive levels of household debt and concerns about the rising cost of living.

A report from the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning US-based think tank focused on economic issues, found that extreme poverty in Brazil fell by about 40 percent between 2022 and 2024, unemployment dropped to historic lows, and the country’s economic growth significantly outpaced that of most of its neighbours. But the analysis also found that households were strained by a sharp uptick in the cost of servicing debt. All in all, analysts say they amount to a view of the economy that is neither catastrophic nor particularly satisfying.

Pagliarini says that both candidates have tried to steer the election onto more favourable terrain for their issues of choice, with Lula portraying Flavio Bolsonaro as a willing accomplice in US efforts to undermine Brazilian sovereignty, and Flavio Bolsonaro accusing Lula of being corrupt and weak on crime.

Analysts say that polls reflect the state of Brazilian politics: deeply polarised but unenthusiastic.

“The general vibe is that this is a very downbeat campaign,” said Pagliarini. “There’s not a lot of enthusiasm either way, and it’s hard to tell at this stage who that favours.”

Most surveys show a close race, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Flavio Bolsonaro that tightens further in a hypothetical run-off.

A Quaest survey from September shows Lula with 37 percent of voter intention against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 33 percent, while an AtlasIntel survey from the same period showed Lula winning 46 percent to Flavio Bolsonaro’s 43 percent.

A Datafolha poll found Lula with 40 percent and Flavio Bolsonaro with 36 percent.

Polls also show Flavio Bolsonaro favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula is seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and health.

What challenges has each campaign faced?

An explosive corruption scandal, focused on disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, has raised questions for both campaigns and implicated members of the country’s political and economic elite across the political spectrum.

Reports found that Flavio Bolsonaro had solicited substantial funds from Vorcaro, ostensibly to finance a documentary – The Dark Horse (or O Azarao) – about his father.

Lula’s former finance minister, Guido Mantega, has also said he helped arrange a meeting with Vorcaro, Lula and the head of Brazil’s central bank to discuss banking policy. Lula has said he told Vorcaro there would be no political interference in his bank’s case, only a “technical investigation conducted by the central bank”. The Reuters news agency confirmed the meeting.

The scandal has also embroiled the country’s Supreme Court , with Alexandre de Moraes, whose central role in Bolsonaro’s coup trial turned him into a subject of ire for the political right, facing questions about his own links to the banker.

De Moraes has in turn accused a justice appointed by Bolsonaro of wrongdoing, with the court considering probes into the conduct of both justices.

What are the concerns about US intervention?

Concerns that the Trump administration could intervene or seek to influence the outcome on behalf of Bolsonaro have also loomed over the election.

The US president has frequently threatened to cut off economic assistance to Latin American countries if his preferred candidate fails to win. Trump had also used sanctions to target members of the Brazilian judiciary involved in the case against the elder Bolsonaro, which he portrayed as a “witch-hunt”. Trump also placed heavy tariffs on Brazil in a bid to have the case thrown out.

The country’s government denied visas to two US officials who sought to travel to Brazil, saying they planned to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazilian elections. Lula’s government has warned the US against meddling in the country’s domestic affairs.

Trump has himself used false claims of rampant fraud to justify efforts to remain in office despite his election loss in 2020.

A group of 31 Democratic US Congress members recently sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticising “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazilian elections.

The Reuters reported that Brazilian intelligence officials also briefed a French and German delegation in September about possible interference in the election by outside powers such as the US and Russia. The officials said that US interference ranged “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged”.

articles.title: At least 17 people, mostly pilgrims, killed in Kenya road crash
articles.summary: The multi-vehicle crash occurred in the Salama area, 90km southeast of Nairobi, killing mostly Catholic pilgrims.
articles.body:
At least 17 people, most of them Catholic pilgrims on the way to a prayer site, have been killed in a crash involving multiple vehicles on the highway to the Kenyan coastal city of Mombasa.

The crash in the Salama area, about 90 kilometres (about 55 miles) southeast of the capital Nairobi, happened after midnight, police said on Saturday.

The crash occurred when a truck driver tried and failed to overtake another truck; that caused a collision with vehicles including a van carrying pilgrims, police said.

Kenyan media reported that the pilgrims were travelling in a 14-seater minibus.

The van’s driver and 16 passengers, most of them women, died at the scene, police said.

The pilgrims were going to a prayer site in Nakuru County, west of Nairobi, said Martin Kivuva, archbishop of the Catholic Archdiocese of Mombasa.

The archbishop said in a statement that he and others were “saddened with lots of grief” over the deaths.

President William Ruto offered condolences to the families, friends, parishioners and the entire Catholic community “who are mourning this painful loss”.

Kenya’s National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) launched an investigation into the crash.

The NTSA said it dispatched investigators “to establish the full circumstances leading to the collision”.

But it noted that the stretch of road where the crash occurred is a known “black spot” and that “recommendations have been made to address safety concerns” regarding the route.

Road accidents are a problem across Africa. In Kenya and elsewhere in the region, the accidents are often blamed on poorly maintained vehicles, excess speed and poor road conditions.

Kenya recorded 5,009 road traffic deaths last year, while 2,150 deaths were reported in the first six months of 2026, local media reported, citing numbers from the NTSA.

articles.title: Trump's attempted assassin sent mysterious texts about 3D printer leading up to Butler, Pa. shooting: report
articles.summary: FBI records obtained by Judicial Watch reveal Thomas Matthew Crooks sent cryptic coded texts and took drone photos of Pittsburgh stadiums before the attack
articles.body: Thomas Matthew Crooks, the shooter in the assassination attempt at President Donald Trump's Butler, Pennsylvania, rally on July 13, 2024, sent a series of strangely coded text messages in the months leading up to the shooting, according to records obtained by Judicial Watch. "Did you 3D print the parts?" an individual the FBI described as an "unknown contact," messaged Crooks on Feb. 9, 2023. "Yes, except for the fan blades," Crooks responded. "Woah that looks cool," the unknown contact replied to Crooks, also asking about the "parts" in response to a Crooks message which the FBI redacted. GOP LAWMAKERS BLINDSIDED BY NEW REVELATIONS ABOUT TRUMP BUTLER SHOOTER: 'AWFULLY STRANGE' ATTEMPTED TRUMP ASSASSIN THOMAS CROOKS’ BEHAVIOR REVEALED ‘RED FLAGS’ BEFORE ATTACK: FORMER FBI AGENT Another series of messages between Crooks and a redacted second party display a series of odd one- or two-word messages Crooks sent the contact between May 21, 2023, and Jan. 3, 2024. "Hello … Hello red …Hello red … Hdudhdbdbbd … 7888ejdj … Yolo … Ddodjjf … 890 … Hdjd … Djdj … red … Yup red … Hello … Jhhhuuh … Hhdj … Jjjjjjjjjjjj … Hello red … Red red," Crooks' messages read. The FBI redacted any potential response from the other party, according to the documents. Other information Judicial Watch received from the FBI documents included a notification from shipping company DHL about a package Crooks received from Hong Kong. ATTEMPTED TRUMP ASSASSIN THOMAS CROOKS USED 'BOB DOLE' ALIAS BEFORE ANONYMOUS DONOR PAID FOR CREMATION: DOCS The document release also included 40 drone photos Crooks took between Feb. 6, 2024, and Feb. 27, 2024, which included photos of PNC Park and Acrisure Stadium, where the MLB's Pittsburgh Pirates and the NFL's Pittsburgh Steelers play, respectively. Crooks' affinity for 3D printing had been previously reported by the New York Post, after the outlet reviewed a series of documents obtained by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa. UKRAINIAN NATIONAL WHO COMPLETED AIR FORCE OFFICER TRAINING CONVICTED IN GHOST GUN 3D PRINTING OPERATION Crooks had previously attempted to use his 3D printer to create a Glock 19 handgun, his father, Matthew Crooks, told investigators, according to the documents obtained by Grassley. "Using carbon fiber plastic, a dryer and a toaster oven, Thomas did once create a Glock 19," Matthew Crooks told investigators. BLUE STATE GOVERNORS JOIN GUN-GRABBING EFFORTS BY TARGETING GLOCK PISTOLS But, fearing the gun would explode, Matthew Crooks forbade his son from using it, according to records obtained by the Post. Crooks' assassination attempt on then-candidate Donald Trump, while unsuccessful in killing Trump, resulted in the deaths of two civilians. Corey Comperatore, a 50-year-old fire chief, died immediately while shielding his family from bullets. TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS James Copenhaver, a 76-year-old veteran, was shot in the triceps and the midsection, receiving injuries to vital organs including his kidneys and colon. Though Copenhaver was released from the hospital a week after the shooting, he dealt with complications from the injuries in the ensuing years. On Sept. 23, 2026, he died due to those complications. articles.title: Noel Gallagher guitar sells for £12,000 at Oasis auction
articles.summary: The instrument was one of a number of items which belonged to a former Oasis sound engineer.
articles.body:
A guitar which originally belonged to Noel Gallagher has been sold for £12,000 at auction.

The limited edition Epiphone instrument in Manchester City blue was one of a number of items put up for sale by the son of Huw Richards, a former front-of-house sound engineer with the band.

Another of the items in his collection, a Kangol rain jacket produced for the band's touring personnel, sold for £2,000.

But a set of unheard Oasis recordings valued at between £1.2m and £1.6m were pulled from the auction last week , after the band filed an injunction.

That collection of recordings, known as The Desk Tapes, includes recordings of 63 live shows, soundchecks and more than 100 hours of rehearsals from the band's rise and rise in the 1990s.

Littleton Auctions in Worcestershire, which handled the auction, said it had agreed to postpone the sale until the legal dispute had been resolved.

The Epiphone guitar was made in 1997 and the auctioneer said it is believed to be one of five identical guitars gifted to Noel Gallagher by the manufacturer.

It was later given to Richards, Littleton Auctions said.

A collection of 11 framed platinum discs, from the Oasis album What's the Story Morning Glory which also belonged to Richards sold for £2,000.

They had been presented to him by Creation Records to recognise United Kingdom sales of more than 3.3 million copies.

Other items in the Richards collection to sell at the auction included tour itineraries, promotional material and a Be Here Now wrist watch.

A number of other sellers also had memorabilia up for sale at the auction, including a rare original concert ticket for The Rain, the Manchester band which later became Oasis.

That sold for £2,400 and an early Oasis demo tape sold for £3,600.

A collection of early Oasis photos sold for £5,400 and a pair of leather shoes which once belonged to Noel Gallagher sold for £1,200.

But a baby grand piano which featured in the artwork for the Supersonic single, which was valued at between £100,000 and £150,000 failed to sell.

articles.title: Tens of thousands protest in Spain after failed housing reforms
articles.summary: Latest demonstrations deepen a days-long crisis after parliament struck down two affordable housing decrees.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people are rallying across Spain to demand affordable housing measures, the day after members of parliament rejected an emergency relief package for tenants.

Demonstrators took to the streets in the capital, Madrid, and about 50 other cities on Saturday, calling for a general strike and reforms to address the country’s increasingly expensive housing market.

On Friday, the Spanish parliament voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing government that intended to quell the crisis.

“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, told the Reuters news agency while protesting in Madrid. “It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”

Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.

The eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her Madrid home triggered the movement more than a week ago, as hundreds set up tents in central Madrid to push for reforms.

“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.

In the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police ousted them.

Protests in dozens of other cities were peaceful, as people waved signs with slogans such as “Houses to live in, a planet to inhabit” and “the right to a roof”.

Friday’s vote was a blow to Spanish leader Sanchez, who heads a coalition government made up of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar.

The two measures were scrapped after the right-wing Catalan separatist party Junts voted against them, arguing they would tighten the housing market.

Junts joined the main opposition Popular Party (PP) and the far-right Vox party in downing the measures.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged Sanchez after the vote to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.

Spanish media reported on Friday that Sanchez would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision.

Sanchez’s office did not comment on the reports.

articles.summary: An Indian national with Green Card, Yogesh Chandaben Dabhi, filed a petition stating that he is a lawful permanent resident of the US, but he was detained
articles.body: An Indian national with Green Card, Yogesh Chandaben Dabhi, filed a petition stating that he is a lawful permanent resident of the US, but he was detained when he was returning to India as "an alien". The petition was filed in July, which prompted the administration to file a reply explaining why a Green Card holder was detained. The government produced two past judgments of conviction in which the Indian national received sentences totaling seven years of confinement. The administration said his detention was lawful because he had been convicted of two or more offences.Here's what happenedThe man, Yogesh Chandaben Dabhi, is a lawful permanent resident (green-card holder). He challenged his detention in federal court.The US government said Dabhi had two criminal convictions, with prison sentences adding up to seven years. Because of those convictions, the government considered him inadmissible to the US under immigration law.Normally, a green-card holder has the right to live in the US. But immigration law has an important exception: in certain situations, a returning green-card holder can be treated as someone trying to enter the US for the first time — legally called an "applicant for admission."That distinction mattered because it allowed the government to argue that Dabhi could be held in mandatory immigration detention while his immigration case continued.What did Dabhi argue?Dabhi argued that the government could not simply treat him as an applicant for admission and detain him without giving him a chance to challenge his detention.He asked the federal court to order his release.But while his federal case was going on, Dabhi admitted in immigration court that the facts in the government's case were true and that he was inadmissible because of his criminal convictions. That weakened his argument against detention.What did the judge decide?The judge sided with the government. The court said the government could use 8 USC §1225(b)(2)(A) to detain Dabhi because of his immigration status and criminal history. The judge also rejected Dabhi's argument that his detention violated his constitutional right to due process.What happened to his case?The judge:rejected Dabhi's request to be released;granted the government's request for summary judgment;dismissed Dabhi's case with prejudice.In simple terms, Dabhi lost this particular federal court challenge to his detention.Why is this important?The case is relevant to Green Card holders with criminal records who leave the US and later return. It shows that having a green card does not always mean a person will simply be admitted back into the US without an immigration inspection or detention risk.However, this ruling does not mean every green-card holder returning to America can be detained without a bond hearing. articles.title: Portadown: Rallies take place in Portadown over Drumcree dispute
articles.summary: The fallout over the proposed march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.
articles.body:
Rallies are being held in Portadown on both sides of the Drumcree parade dispute as the stand-off between Garvaghy Road residents and the Orange Order continues.

It comes after the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said a "major public safety operation" will continue in Portadown this weekend.

Speaking at an event on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister and Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O'Neill said she heard the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant "talk about being between a rock and a hard place", adding she has "never heard such nonsense, this is between right and wrong".

Speaking at Drumcree church, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart repeated calls for PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher and his officers to "do their job" and facilitate the parade, describing the current impasse as "mob rule".

The fallout over the proposed march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.

Huge crowds have turned up on the Garvaghy Road on Saturday to support local residents.

A smaller event is being held in the Edgarstown area in Portadown in support of the Orange Order.

O'Neill said that "if this British government isn't prepared to end this crisis, then it's up to the thousands here, to collectively stand with the Garvaghy Road residents".

She said: "We will stand shoulder to shoulder for as long as it takes."

People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll told the event that "earlier this year they came for migrants, now they're coming for the residents of the Garvaghy Road".

Former SDLP MLA Dolores Kelly said: "Never again did we think we'd be on the Garvaghy Road again to say no going back and no Orange Order parades in the Garvaghy Road."

Speaking to BBC News NI at Drumcree, Lockhart said there could be "repercussions for a very long time if mob rule wins over the rule of law".

Asked if we had stepped back from the "abyss" cited by both Lockhart and a High Court Judge in reference to last week's court proceedings, Lockhart was firm that no progress had yet been made.

"No, we need the police service to step up and do their job. I do think if the real residents step forward we can and should discuss further options and resolutions, because we do want to see this resolved," Lockhart said.

"Where I see the abyss is for the PSNI. It needs community and political support and if they allow mob rule to win in NI, I think we are staring down the abyss in terms of confidence in the rule of law."

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said he was "concerned at the prolonged standoff" which he said was "ultimately in nobody's interests".

"I have been working with all those involved to find a mutually acceptable solution," he said in a social media post on Saturday.

He said he was grateful to those engaging in dialogue, adding that it was "a crucial time" for Northern Ireland and he hoped compromise could be found.

"Leadership is never easy at moments like this but I commend all those who are trying to get to a solution."

A spokesperson for Fianna Fáil said the taoiseach believes "now is a time for us to be calm and careful in what we say", adding there is a "history of hurt around Drumcree".

They said: "While no agreement has been reached, it is crucial that channels of communication remain open."

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded

The PSNI said it was "continuing to seek safe and peaceful compliance" with the Parades Commission's decision that the Orange Order parade could go ahead with restrictions.

On Wednesday, the PSNI Chief Constable said there would be an investigation after protesters blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent the parade from happening.

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said on Friday that the "investigation into anyone suspected of breaking the law related to this dispute is continuing at pace".

He added that the PSNI are doing "everything we can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone" in Portadown.

"I want to thank those officers from Police Services in England and Scotland who have been in Northern Ireland supporting our efforts over the past week," he added.

"Finally, I want to repeat the Chief Constable's appeal for calm and for all parties to refocus efforts on working to find a lasting resolution to this issue."

Protesters have remained on Garvaghy Road and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday.

A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday.

Meanwhile just after 22:00 BST on Friday, Portadown Orangemen made another attempt to parade down the Garvaghy Road.

As has been the case with repeated attempts this week, a senior PSNI officer stopped them at the bottom of Drumcree Hill.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years.

The row re-emerged last month after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application to parade was lodged.

Last Friday, the commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.

However, that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go-ahead just hours before it was due to take place .

articles.title: Middlesbrough Turner Prize workshops hope to inspire youngsters
articles.summary: Thousands of school children from across the Tees Valley visit Mima art gallery to be inspired.
articles.body:
School children have been taking part in workshops inspired by this year's Turner Prize nominated artworks.

Teesside University's Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art (MIMA) is hosting work by four artists in the running for the prestigious award - Simeon Barclay, Kira Freije, Marguerite Humeau and Tanoa Sasraku.

Around 17,000 youngsters across the Tees Valley have been signed up to the Turner on Tees schools programme which involves artist-led workshops.

Senior learning curator at MIMA, Claire Pounder, said they hoped to inspire "cultural confidence and capital" and get young people visiting galleries.

The Turner Prize is awarded each year to a British artist for an outstanding exhibition or other presentation of their work.

Speaking during a workshop with Brambles Primary Academy, based in the town, Pounder said: "When you get here, you're wondering, you're philosophical, you're asking questions, you're challenging.

"It's literally the spirit of the Turner Prize."

Year 4 pupils Muhammed thought the art "looked cool", whereas his classmate Holly thought it "looked kind of strange".

Elsie added: "We've had a lot of fun, and we're excited about what's coming next."

Chief executive of Tees Valley education multi academy trust, Katrina Morley, said such opportunities allowed children to flourish.

"Our children and young people are the future of our communities, and so as custodians we're showing them where they might want to go next."

The Turner Prize exhibition at MIMA runs until 29 March 2027. The winner will be announced on 10 December 2026 .

articles.body: Patna: The Bihar Industrial Area Development Authority (Biada) on Saturday approved allotment of 9.14 acres of industrial land and plug-and-play sheds to 12 industrial units. articles.title: A forest through the eyes of the deaf
articles.summary: Inclusive nature walk in Chennai’s Nanmangalam forest lets deaf participants explore flora and insects through photography with sign-language interpreters.
articles.body: “Tt is so quiet out here,” was what one of the hearing impaired participants observed, on taking a walk through Nanmangalam forest. It was 7am and there was just the chirping of birds and insects to be heard. “For people with hearing impairment who use hearing aids, the urban soundscape can sometimes become overwhelmingly loud,” says Anjana Venkatecan of Care Earth Trust, which collaborated with the Deaf Artists Collective (DFC) to conduct the nature walk recently, along with the Tamil Nadu forest department. “Being able to access a peaceful place and experience the sounds of nature was a big deal for them,” she says.DFC, a creative community initiative under Madras Photo Bloggers, aims to bridge the accessibility gap by creating meaningful and dignified opportunities for deaf people to explore various spaces. Though they have had photo walks before, this is the first exclusive nature walk for the deaf to be conducted with their communication needs in mind. “When it is primarily a photo walk, participants may be more interested in photography than in learning about the environment,” says Anjana. “Having sign language interpretation and a deaf-friendly environment made it easier for them to participate, learn, connect with others and enjoy the experience without worrying about communication barriers.”Srivatsan Sankaran, founder of Madras Photo Bloggers, says many deaf people do not always get opportunities to experience and capture nature because of communication and accessibility barriers. “Most outdoor activities and nature experiences are designed around hearing-based communication. Information may be given verbally, instructions may be announced without visual alternatives, and sign language interpretation may not be available. We wanted participants to explore and experience nature through photography.”Nanmangalam is a forested area and so spotting birds was difficult, says Anjana. “That gave us an opportunity to talk more about its flora. The walk was more geared towards insects. We saw a lot of butterflies, stick insects, weaver ants and other insects.”The sign-language interpreter is crucial to the experience. “From our side, we had to slightly change our approach to accommodate the interpretation, slow down and factor in the additional time required for signing,” says Anjana.DFC will continue creating more of such inclusive nature walks and photography experiences for the deaf community in different environments, says Srivatsan.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news.
